intro: Lyon keeps a formal, published list of its remarkable trees: four carry the national Arbre Remarquable label, and one park holds the collective Ensemble Arboré Remarquable label for its whole 8,800-tree collection. That park, the Tête d'Or, exists because 19th century Lyonnais wanted a green space to rival Paris's Bois de Boulogne, and two Swiss brothers gave them one with species from four continents. What survives elsewhere is quieter: a giant chestnut in a half-wild park, a cedar on a Saône island where monks gardened for a thousand years, an oak collection planted the year before the First World War.
meta_description: Lyon labels its remarkable trees by law. Meet a pine first grown in Europe via Kew in 1856, a giant chestnut, and an island cedar monks once tended.
question_answer: Lyon has no single documented oldest tree, but its most precisely dated remarkable tree is the Pin de Bunge, also called the Pin de Napoléon, in the Parc de la Tête d'Or, planted around 1856 during the park's creation and now roughly 170 years old. It carries France's national Arbre Remarquable label and is described by the label association as having no equivalent elsewhere in the country.
question_meta: Lyon's most precisely dated remarkable tree is an 1856 Chinese pine in Parc de la Tête d'Or. Its story, exact location, and twelve more remarkable trees.
question_context: Lyon is one of the few cities on this list with an actual published inventory to work from: the city government maintains a list of nationally labelled Arbres Remarquables, awarded by the A.R.B.R.E.S. association, and the Metropole publishes open data on protected trees across Greater Lyon. That inventory favours species rarity, size and documented planting circumstances over sheer age, which is why the Pin de Bunge, a Chinese species first introduced to Europe through Kew Gardens in the 19th century, anchors this list rather than an oak or a yew. It stands along the perimeter path of the Tête d'Or's arboretum, a five minute walk from the Boulevard des Belges entrance, in a park that itself holds France's Ensemble Arboré Remarquable label for the whole collection. Older individual claims exist elsewhere in the city, a cedar on the Saône island of Île Barbe where monks are documented gardening for over a thousand years, but none carry the same precisely dated planting record the Pin de Bunge does.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Lyon?
faq.a: No single tree in Lyon has a formally documented single oldest claim. The most precisely dated remarkable tree is the Pin de Bunge in Parc de la Tête d'Or, planted around 1856 during the park's creation, now roughly 170 years old.

faq.q: Why does Parc de la Tête d'Or have so many rare trees?
faq.a: It was designed from 1856 by Swiss landscape architects Eugène and Denis Bühler as a full arboretum alongside a public park, and absorbed Lyon's old botanical garden collection in 1857, giving it species pulled from four continents rather than the usual local mix.

faq.q: How does Lyon protect its remarkable trees?
faq.a: Through the national Arbre Remarquable label, awarded by the A.R.B.R.E.S. association, which four individual Lyon trees currently hold, and through the Metropole's own urban plan (PLU), which flags protected trees and wooded areas on open data maps.

faq.q: Are Lyon's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Yes. All of them are free to see with no entry fee, from the island garden of Île Barbe, reachable on foot via a footbridge over the Saône, to a rare oak on an ordinary Villeurbanne street corner.

trees.name: The Pin de Bunge, or Pin de Napoléon

location.address: Parc de la Tête d'Or, arboretum perimeter path, 69006 Lyon

trees.story: This pine's bark peels in patches of grey, green and cream as it ages, a trait so distinctive that the species barely needs its Latin name to identify it. Pinus bungeana is native to central China, first documented for Western science by the Russian botanist Alexander von Bunge in 1831 at a temple garden in Beijing, and this specimen was probably planted in 1856, the year construction began on the Parc de la Tête d'Or itself, making it one of the park's original plantings rather than a later addition. The International Dendrology Society's own reference site names it directly as the oldest cultivated Pinus bungeana in Europe, calling it a national treasure of the Lyon botanical garden, a specific claim rather than a vague superlative, and one this project treats as credible given the source. Locally it carries the nickname Pin de Napoléon, though no source connects the name to any specific historical event rather than general period association, so that link is not claimed here as fact. Nearly 170 years on, its trunk has developed the pale, almost white patchwork bark that only develops with real age, the single feature that makes this pine worth seeking out among the arboretum's thousands of other specimens.

trees.transport: 10 min walk from Masséna metro station (Line A)
trees.notes: The 'Pin de Napoléon' nickname's origin is not documented in any source checked; not claimed as connected to Napoleon himself, only reported as a local name. A matching photo exists on Flickr (user Michele 69600) but is marked All Rights Reserved, not a usable open licence, so not used per hard rule 4. Photo viewed directly: shows a multi-trunked pine with distinctive pale, mottled grey-cream-green patchwork bark, exactly the trait the story describes, beside a small park information sign. Approved.

trees.name: The Osage Orange of the Tête d'Or

location.address: Parc de la Tête d'Or, arboretum, 69006 Lyon

trees.story: This tree's American ancestors were weapons before they were shade. Maclura pomifera is named for the Osage nation of the central United States, who prized its wood, dense, springy and rot-resistant, for war bows and arrows above almost any other timber available to them. The species reached Europe in 1823, and French growers in the south of the country initially planted it not for its odd, wrinkled, inedible fruit but as living fencing and, briefly, as a food source for silkworms before mulberry proved more practical. This specimen in the Tête d'Or's arboretum has grown into something closer to a specimen tree than a hedge. A dendrologist's survey put its girth at 3.70 metres a metre above the ground, with a trunk described as ridged and hollowed over some two metres of its height, reasonably read as the marks of a genuinely old, over-a-century specimen rather than a fast-growing recent planting. Osage orange also spreads by layering, sending down roots wherever a low branch touches soil, so what looks like one tree in a dense stand may in places be a single genetic individual repeating itself.

trees.transport: 10 min walk from Masséna metro station (Line A)
trees.notes: Age given as 'plus que centenaire' (over a century) by the dendrology source rather than a precise figure, based on girth and trunk condition rather than a documented planting record. trees.name: The Bald Cypress of the Tête d'Or

best_time.label: November, when its needles turn copper and drop, the one month it truly looks like the Louisiana wetlands it comes from

location.address: Parc de la Tête d'Or, near the lake, 69006 Lyon

trees.story: This tree grows as though it remembers the Louisiana wetlands its species comes from, even landlocked in a Lyon park more than eight thousand kilometres away. Taxodium distichum is one of the few conifers that sheds its needles every autumn, and where it grows in standing water, it sends up woody knees, called pneumatophores, that poke above the surface to bring oxygen to submerged roots, a trait this specimen displays even without the flooded ground its Gulf Coast relatives depend on. A dendrological survey recorded its girth at 5.45 metres a metre above ground and its height at just over 30 metres, among the largest measured trees anywhere in the park's arboretum, with a deeply fluted, buttressed trunk in excellent health. No source gives it a specific planting date, so its age is estimated here from the park's own founding in the 1850s rather than documented directly, but a tree of this size, in a species not known for exceptionally fast growth, is a serious candidate for one of the arboretum's oldest original plantings.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Masséna metro station (Line A)
trees.notes: No documented planting date; age estimated from the park's 1850s founding given the tree's exceptional measured size (5.45m girth, 30.5m height) rather than a verified record. trees.name: The Giant Chestnut of Parc de la Garde

best_time.label: May, when its candle-shaped flower spikes cover the canopy

location.address: Parc de la Garde, 6 Rue de la Garde, 69005 Lyon

trees.story: Most visitors to this park come for the wildness rather than any single tree, but the chestnut at its centre is the reason locals bother naming the place at all. Parc de la Garde keeps a half-forested character unusual for a Lyon city park: its lower half is genuinely wooded, criss-crossed by informal paths, and holds a small stone bridge that once carried the old Vaugneray tramway line through the woods before the route was abandoned. The horse chestnut standing among these trees has been formally recognised with France's national Arbre Remarquable label, described locally simply as an enormous trunk carrying multiple large branches, a scale that marks it out even among the park's other mature trees. No source gives the tree an individual age or measured girth beyond that general description, so any figure here is an estimate rather than a documented record. The label itself, rather than any dramatic history, is what distinguishes this specimen from the thousands of ordinary horse chestnuts planted across French parks in the 19th and 20th centuries.

trees.name: The Japanese Pagoda Tree of Parc de Gerland

best_time.label: August, when it flowers later than almost anything else still blooming in the park

location.address: Parc de Gerland, 24 Allée Pierre de Coubertin, 69007 Lyon

trees.story: Gerland is one of Lyon's newer large parks by name, built out on former industrial and marshland south of the city centre and reworked repeatedly through the 20th century, so a tree old enough to carry a national remarkable-tree label stands out by contrast with almost everything else growing around it. In 2024 the A.R.B.R.E.S. association added this Japanese pagoda tree to its national list, formally measuring it at 16 metres tall with an 18 metre crown spread and a trunk 302 centimetres around at chest height, figures precise enough to track any future growth or decline against. Despite the common name, the species is native to China rather than Japan, introduced to Europe in the 18th century and prized since for flowering late in summer when few other large trees are still blooming, a trait that makes it valuable to bees and other pollinators after the main spring flush has finished. No individual planting date is documented, so the tree's age is estimated here from its measured size rather than a verified record, but the label recognition alone marks it as one of the more significant individual trees in a 40 hectare park built mainly for sport and recreation rather than horticulture.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of Parc de la Chapelle
trees.age_estimate: locally claimed at 500 years, botanically disputed

location.address: Parc de la Chapelle, 18 Rue de la Chapelle, 69009 Lyon

trees.story: This cedar is effectively the reason the park around it exists in its current shape: much of Parc de la Chapelle is built around a single enormous specimen, with the site's open lawn and paths arranged to give the tree room rather than the other way around. Measured at 28 metres tall with a 32 metre crown spread and a trunk 6.35 metres around, it received France's national Arbre Remarquable label on 16 October 2024, and city sources describe it as multi-centenary, some putting a figure of around 500 years on it directly. That number sits awkwardly against the species' own history: Cedrus atlantica, native to the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria, was not introduced into French cultivation until the 1840s, which would make a genuinely 500-year-old specimen growing in a Lyon park difficult to reconcile with any documented planting. The claim is stated here as what it is, a locally repeated figure rather than a settled fact, alongside the tree's real, independently confirmed scale and its 2024 national label. Whatever its true age, it is locally described as possibly the largest Atlas cedar in Lyon, and its branches shelter birds and squirrels in a quiet residential corner of the 9th arrondissement.

trees.name: The Oak Collection of Parc de la Cerisaie

location.address: Parc de la Cerisaie, Rue Chazière, 69004 Lyon

trees.story: This park takes its name from a cherry orchard that no longer exists, replaced just before the First World War by a very different planting scheme. Landscape architect René-Edouard André, son of the more famous Édouard André whose formal garden style shaped parks across France and beyond, designed Parc de la Cerisaie in 1913 on the Croix-Rousse hillside, centring the roughly 1,200-tree planting on a significant oak collection alongside birches, yews and beeches. That timing puts the park's founding trees at just over a century old today, planted the year before the war that would go on to reshape the neighbourhood and the city around them. No individual tree in the collection carries a separately documented age or measurement, so the range given here describes the park's own founding date rather than any single named specimen, consistent with how this project treats other undated group plantings. What survives is less a single monumental tree than a coherent, deliberately designed early 20th century woodland, unusually intact for a century-old civic planting scheme.

trees.name: The Garden Trees of Jardin des Chartreux

location.address: Jardin des Chartreux, Montée des Chartreux, 69004 Lyon

trees.story: This garden sits on the steep slope between the Croix-Rousse plateau and the Saône, on ground once attached to a Carthusian monastery that gave the neighbourhood its name and that disappeared, like most French religious houses of its kind, during the Revolution. What remains today is a public garden of broad lawns and mature trees, magnolia, cedar and horse chestnut among the species named in descriptions of the site, arranged to take advantage of a genuinely striking view over the Saône quays and the hills of Fourvière on the opposite bank. No individual tree here has a documented planting date or measurement, and no single specimen is singled out by name the way the labelled trees elsewhere on this list are, so this entry describes the garden's mature tree cover as a group rather than claiming one named champion. The steep terrain that makes the view worthwhile also keeps the garden genuinely quiet, a local rather than a tourist destination, reached by a climb up from the river that most visitors to Lyon never make.

trees.name: The Cappadocian Maple of the Tête d'Or

location.address: Parc de la Tête d'Or, arboretum, 69006 Lyon

trees.story: This maple comes from a stretch of the world most visitors to a French municipal park have never had reason to think about: the mountain forests running from the Caucasus through northern Iran and on toward the Himalayas, where Acer cappadocicum grows wild among beech and oak. Lyon's botanical garden, folded into the Tête d'Or since 1857, was built to hold exactly this kind of geographic range, species chosen for scientific and educational value as much as for looks. A dendrological survey of the park recorded this specimen's girth at 3.20 metres a metre above ground and its height at 26 metres, respectable rather than record-breaking figures next to the arboretum's largest specimens, but enough to mark it as a genuinely mature, long-established tree rather than a recent planting. No individual planting date is documented, so its age is estimated here from its measured size and the arboretum's own founding period rather than a verified record. In autumn its leaves turn a clean, even yellow, a display Cappadocian maples are specifically valued for in cultivation, though no source dates this specimen's colour peak precisely enough to state a reliable calendar window here.

trees.name: The Pedunculate Oak of Rue Viret

location.address: Corner of Rue Viret and Rue Francis de Pressense, Les Poulettes / Gratte-Ciel, 69100 Villeurbanne
location.neighbourhood: Villeurbanne (Les Poulettes, adjoining Gratte-Ciel), roughly 1.4 km east of Parc de la Tete d'Or

trees.story: Villeurbanne's official tree register calls this pedunculate oak rare, and it means it plainly: street plantings here run to plane and lime, so a full-grown Quercus robur on a residential corner stands out as an exception the city itself has flagged. The 2017 survey that logged it recorded good health and real size and nothing else, no planting date, no measured age, just a note that this one was worth watching. An investigative piece on Lyon's remarkable trees found it again in 2025, still standing at the same corner of Rue Viret and Rue Francis de Pressense, eight years on from that first record. It grows a fifteen minute walk from the Art Deco tower blocks of Gratte-Ciel, Villeurbanne's landmark 1930s housing project, in the quieter grid of streets just west of it. Nobody has measured its trunk or dated its rings, so this page will not guess a number rather than invent one. What two independent records agree on is simpler: an oak grown too large and too old to belong on an ordinary street, still there, still worth the detour from the park at the Tete d'Or.

trees.name: The Anne Frank Chestnut

location.address: Place Marc-Aron, rue Moncey, 69003 Lyon

trees.story:
This chestnut is not old. It is barely twelve, planted at the centre of Place Marc-Aron in December 2014 to replace a statue called Renaissance that the square's renovation had removed. What makes it worth a stop is where it comes from: it is a cutting from the horse chestnut Anne Frank could see through the attic window of her hiding place in Amsterdam, the tree she described in her diary as one of the only things connecting her to the outside world.

That original tree fell in a storm on 23 August 2010. Before it went, the Anne Frank Foundation had already taken roughly 150 cuttings and sent saplings to institutions and public spaces worldwide, Washington DC, Jerusalem and Paris among them, so the tree from the diary kept growing in dozens of places after the original one did not. Lyon's arrived on rue Moncey in a public ceremony and now stands in a small square two minutes' walk from Place Guichard metro station, marked by nothing more than its own planting.

It will not be Lyon's oldest or largest tree for a very long time, maybe not ever. It is here because of what it descends from rather than what it has personally witnessed, the one entry on this list whose whole story predates its own roots.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Place Antoine-Rivoire

location.address: Place Antoine-Rivoire, 69002 Lyon

trees.story:
Lyon's street-tree database holds over 100,000 records, and barely more than half of them carry a planting date at all. Of the ones that do, this plane is the oldest: put in the ground in 1894, at the centre of a square barely bigger than a tennis court in the heart of the Presqu'ile. A city forestry official is on record saying plainly that none of Lyon's plane trees reach the three or four centuries some regional specimens do, so call this the oldest dated tree in the city's records rather than its oldest tree outright.

The square itself has buried more history than its tree has years. From the 16th century until the French Revolution it was the parish cemetery of Saint-Nizier, the church that still stands two streets over. The Revolution cleared the cemetery, and the square that replaced it was called Place de la Fromagerie until 1934, when it was renamed for Antoine Rivoire, a founder of Lyon's trade fair and tourism board.

The plane tree stands alone at the centre of it now, at the junction of four small streets, on ground that spent three centuries as a burial ground before anyone planted anything there at all.

trees.name: The Cedar of Square Gabrielle Dupond-Ebrard

location.address: Square Gabrielle Dupond-Ebrard, 28-29 rue des Aqueducs, 69005 Lyon (Point du Jour)

trees.story:
The square's namesake hid people from the Gestapo two streets from here. Gabrielle Dupond-Ebrard lived at 13 avenue du Point du Jour until 1985, working with the Combat resistance network under Pierre Guillain de Benouville, and her house served as a secretariat and shelter for refugees during the German occupation. Lyon later named this small square after her, and the cedar growing in it now outranks almost everything else about the place: a local streets guide calls it simply the square's main feature.

Nobody has measured it. The city's own register of remarkable trees lists it only as a very large specimen, with no planting year and no girth on file, unusual for a species normally easy to date from its own architecture. Cedar of Lebanon grows a tiered, almost horizontal branch structure as it ages, each level wider than the one above it, so the size the register does record is at least visible rather than guessed.

The square sits about 450 metres from the giant chestnut of Parc de la Garde, already on this list, so the two make an easy pair on the same walk through Point du Jour. If you know how old this cedar is, or can get a tape around the trunk, tell us.

trees.story:
In a square of ordinary planes, one has twice the waistline of its neighbours. The Métropole's surveyors measured this London plane on Place Ollier in September 2025 at 545 centimetres round and 31 metres tall. The next biggest tree within 55 metres comes to 265 centimetres. Same species, same square, same street care, and one trunk equals two of the others put together.

In human terms, three adults with their arms spread wide would not quite close a ring around it. At 31 metres it would top a ten-storey building. The crown is surprisingly compact for that height, about 12 metres across, so the tree reads less as a canopy over the square than as a column rising out of it.

Why this one outgrew the rest is not on record. Nobody has published when it was planted, and the planting year in the city's own inventory is an estimate rather than a document, so this page gives it no age. What the record does give is freshness. The survey that measured it took place in September 2025 and found it standing, which makes it one of the more reliably current entries in Lyon's street-tree data. Its history in the Guillotière is unwritten. If you know when it went in, or anything of its story, tell us.

Black poplars are fast, short-lived trees, which is what makes this pair in Gerland worth the stop. To ring the larger trunk you would need nearly three adults with their arms spread wide. Its crown spans about 20 metres, and because the two trees stand so close, the pair reads from the boulevard as one green mass with two trunks.

How old they are is an open question. Poplars put on girth quickly, so thickness is a poor clock for them, and the planting year in the city's inventory is an estimate that sits awkwardly with trunks this size. No planting record has been published, so this page gives them no age rather than a guess.

Stand at the corner of rue Jacques-Louis Hénon and rue Deleuvre and you are looking at them.

They are best understood as a group rather than three separate trees. A cedar of Lebanon on its own spreads its branches wide and level; three planted together at an entrance make an evergreen gateway that holds its shape through every season, while the deciduous trees elsewhere in the square come and go. That is what the register is protecting, the way the trio frames the place as much as the size of any one trunk.

The register gives no measurements and no planting date for them. Nothing on record dates the group, so this page gives it no age. The register entry was last updated in September 2021, and street-level photographs from the corner run up to 2026.

The square has two more protected entries, three copper beeches and a red oak, so it rewards a slow circuit. If you know when the cedars went in, tell us.

trees.story:
Copper beeches are relatively rare around Lyon, the Métropole's register says, and Square Gustave-Auguste Ferrié has three of them together. The register protects them as a very fine group, remarkable both for their size and for that rarity, at the rue Deleuvre corner of the square.

A copper beech is a beech with purple leaves, and the colour changes through the year. The new leaves open purple in spring, darken through the summer and turn coppery before they fall. Three of them side by side make a block of colour, at its strongest in late April and May when the foliage is fresh.

The register does not say how old these are, and gives no girth or height, so this page leaves the age open rather than guessing.

The register entry was last updated in September 2021, and street-level photographs taken near the corner run into 2026. The same square holds three Cedars of Lebanon at its entrance and a big red oak on the rue Hénon side. If you know how long the beeches have stood here, tell us.

trees.name: The Hickory of the Jardin des Chartreux

location.address: Jardin des Chartreux, cours du Général Giraud

trees.story:
The Métropole's register says trees like this one have become rare in Greater Lyon. It protects a large hickory in the Jardin des Chartreux, in good health, on the slope below the Croix-Rousse that once belonged to the Carthusian monastery the garden is named after.

The register's own label is part of the puzzle. It files the tree as Juglans ovoida, with Hickory in quotation marks and Caryer d'Amérique, American hickory, in French. That Latin mixes the walnut genus with what reads like the shagbark hickory, Carya ovata, and no accepted species carries the name as written. Hickories are close relatives of walnuts, so the slip is easy to understand, but it leaves the exact species open. This page calls it a hickory and asks you. If you can tell a shagbark from its cousins, by its bark or its nuts, let us know which it is.

The register gives no height, girth or planting date, so this page gives it no age. Its entry was last updated in June 2016, and street-level photographs near the garden run to early 2026, though none shows this trunk itself. If you find it, a photograph would settle both questions, where exactly it stands and what it is.

The garden is better known for its magnolias, cedars and horse chestnuts. By the register's account, the hickory is the rarer find.

trees.name: The Weeping Blue Cedar of Square Henri Dor, Caluire
trees.species: Blue Weeping Atlas Cedar (Cedrus atlantica 'Glauca Pendula')

location.address: Square Henri Dor, rue du Docteur Henri Dor

trees.story:
The Métropole calls this cedar very rare, and protects it as a single remarkable tree in the landscape for three reasons, its species, its habit and its amplitude. It is a weeping blue Atlas cedar, the cultivar Glauca Pendula, in Square Henri Dor in Caluire-et-Cuire.

The cultivar is a strange tree to meet. An ordinary Atlas cedar grows up and out in tiers. Glauca Pendula grows blue-grey needles on branches that hang straight down, so that an old one looks less like a conifer than a blue curtain. The register picks this one out for its amplitude, the sheer reach of it, which is what makes it worth crossing into Caluire for.

The register does not record its height, its spread in metres or when it was planted, and nothing else on record dates it, so this page gives it no age. The entry was last updated in October 2023, and street-level photographs near the square run into 2026.

Caluire-et-Cuire sits on the plateau just north of the Croix-Rousse, and the square is in the Bissardon neighbourhood. If you visit, tell us how far its branches now reach, and if you know when it went in, tell us that too.

trees.name: The Unpruned Planes of Rue Pierre Termier, Collonges

location.address: Rue Pierre Termier

trees.story:
These two planes have never been pruned since the day they were planted. The Métropole's register of remarkable trees says so in as many words, and adds that a plane grown this way, in its natural shape, is rarely seen anywhere in Greater Lyon.

Most city planes are cut back to fit the street around them, their crowns shaped by whoever last trimmed them. On Rue Pierre Termier in Collonges-au-Mont-d'Or, the register says, the space around these two let them do what a plane does when nobody interferes, and each has built a crown of rare breadth. It calls them very healthy and gives them a long life expectancy still ahead.

That is the reason to come. Not a famous name or a story, but the chance to see what a London plane looks like when it is left alone, two of them about 30 metres apart.

The register gives no height, girth or planting date, so this page gives them no age. Its entry was last updated in September 2021, and street-level photographs at the spot date from October 2022. Collonges is about 12 kilometres up the Saône from central Lyon, near the edge of a comfortable day trip. If you visit, tell us how wide those crowns have grown.

trees.name: The Cedars of Place de la Libération, Écully

location.address: Place de la Libération, beside the mairie

trees.story:
The cedar beside Écully's town hall grew up in the park of an old horticultural estate, and the Métropole's register calls it one of the oldest in the commune. It is a Cedar of Lebanon, protected as a remarkable tree on Place de la Libération, and the register notes its excellent health.

It does not stand alone. About 30 metres away on the same square, a second protected cedar is an Atlas cedar of the blue-needled form, glauca, which the register picks out for its remarkable habit and development. Side by side, the two show how differently two close relatives can grow on one square.

What the horticultural estate grew, and when the cedars went in, the register does not say. Nobody has published a planting date, so this page gives them no age, only the register's word that the Lebanon cedar is among the commune's oldest.

Both register entries were last updated in May 2016. The most recent street-level photographs at the trees are from February 2021, though a photograph of the square taken in August 2026 shows it as it is today. If you visit Écully, tell us both cedars are still there, and send a photograph of each.
